candidate.blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control, printed p. 8 (PDF pageno 11) and Appendix A printed p. 24 (PDF pageno 27): apply principles of infection prevention and educate clients/staff regarding infection-prevention measures; protect clients from health and environmental hazards.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Infection-prevention teaching and early recognition of postoperative infection
candidate.educational_objective: Teach clients after joint replacement to recognize and promptly report wound or joint findings that may indicate surgical or prosthetic joint infection rather than assuming infection risk ends at discharge or requires high fever.

options.A: I will promptly report increasing redness or pain around the incision, cloudy or new wound drainage, increasing joint swelling or persistent worsening pain, or fever because these may indicate infection.
options.B: Drainage and increasing redness are expected during recovery, so I should wait until the joint becomes unusable before contacting the surgical team.
options.C: Once the incision is closed, an implanted joint can no longer become infected, so infection monitoring is needed only in the hospital.
options.D: Persistent joint pain after replacement rules out infection because prosthetic joint infection always causes a high fever before other symptoms appear.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. CDC identifies redness and pain around a surgical site, cloudy wound drainage, and fever as warning findings of surgical site infection, including infections involving implanted material such as a hip replacement. AAOS patient guidance on joint-replacement infection also emphasizes early recognition of incision redness, joint swelling, persistent pain and other infection findings because prosthetic joint infection can require substantial additional treatment. B delays evaluation of concerning wound changes. C is incorrect because prosthetic joint infections can occur after hospital discharge and may present later. D is incorrect because infection does not require a high fever to be present before local or pain-related findings become clinically important. The final item focuses on source-supported postoperative recognition and escalation rather than bundling multiple perioperative prophylaxis protocols into one answer.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Current CDC and AAOS sources directly support recognition and prompt reporting of local wound/joint and systemic findings compatible with infection after joint replacement and establish that implanted material can be involved in SSI.
candidate.source_document_title: Surgical Site Infection Basics; Infection After Joint Replacement
candidate.source_locator: CDC 'Surgical Site Infection Basics' → Overview/Types: SSI can involve implanted material such as a hip replacement; Signs and symptoms: redness and pain around the surgical area, cloudy wound drainage and fever. AAOS OrthoInfo 'Infection After Joint Replacement' → early-recognition guidance: watch for redness at the incision, joint swelling and persistent pain; long-term follow-up is important because some infections can emerge or recur later.
